input:
Case

This proposal sets out the case for electrifying the vehicle fleet, and seeks approval to proceed to the stage of detailed design. The fleet operates out of the depot upon daily rounds of deliveries and site calls, and each and every vehicle returns to the depot at night. It is this pattern which forms the foundation of the case: vehicles returning nightly to a single base may be charged at that base, from charging infrastructure installed once and thereafter used by the fleet as a whole, whilst the daily rounds are of a length comfortably within the range of the electric vehicles presently offered for this class of work. Replacement provides the occasion for the change. The vehicles comprising the fleet reach the end of their working lives in turn, and every replacement is a purchase which will in any event be made; electrification simply takes those purchases as and when they fall due and directs them towards electric vehicles, rather than withdrawing serviceable vehicles from use prematurely. The case does not invite the board to pass judgement upon electric vehicles in the abstract. It invites the board to consider whether the fleet's own particular duty, operated from its own depot, is the species of duty which electric vehicles are well suited to serve, the contention being that the return-to-base pattern in conjunction with the short daily rounds renders it so. What the fleet surrenders in the exchange is the flexibility attaching to a vehicle which may be despatched anywhere at a moment's notice upon a tank replenished in a matter of minutes; the detailed design stage will test the duty records against that loss before any question of purchase is entertained.

Costs

The capital cost amounts to $1016k. The appraisal has been conducted over a horizon of 7 years. The capital cost of $1016k embraces the difference in price between the electric vehicles and the diesel vehicles which they replace, the charging installation at the depot, and such electrical work as the depot supply necessitates in order to support the charging load. Within the horizon, the running costs of the electric fleet are set against those of the diesel fleet which it displaces: electricity as against diesel fuel, and the maintenance of vehicles possessing fewer wearing parts as against the maintenance of engines, gearboxes, and exhaust treatment systems. The savings appearing in the appraisal are estimates, and estimates only. No electric vehicle has as yet been operated upon the fleet's rounds, and the consumption figures underlying the savings are the manufacturers' figures for the class rather than measurements gathered from the fleet's own duty. The appraisal duly records them as estimates, and the first vehicles to enter service will furnish the measured figures against which the remainder of the programme will be judged. Any shortfall in the saving will bear upon the appraisal of every subsequent replacement, each of which is appraised upon an identical basis.

Schedule

Work will commence one quarter after approval has been granted. The first stage comprises the detailed design itself: the duty records of the fleet are to be examined vehicle by vehicle, the depot supply assessed, and the charging layout definitively fixed. Procurement follows upon the design, vehicles being ordered against the replacement dates which the fleet already carries, in such a way that no vehicle is purchased in advance of its predecessor falling due. The charging installation is to be constructed in advance of the arrival of the first electric vehicle, and extended thereafter as the fleet progressively turns over. No contractor is named in this proposal; the installer will be appointed by means of a tender once the design has fixed the installation in detail. The schedule is expressed in terms of stages reckoned from approval for the reason that it is the replacement dates, and not the project, which dictate the pace of the changeover: the fleet becomes electric at the rate at which its vehicles fall due, and at no greater rate.

Decision requested

The decision which is requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and not to the purchase of vehicles. Detailed design will resolve the questions which the case is unable to resolve: which of the vehicles upon the market are capable of covering the fleet's longest rounds with the margin which winter operation demands, whether the depot supply is capable of bearing the charging load of the fleet in its entirety or stands in need of reinforcement, what the charging installation will cost when put out to tender, and what the vehicles themselves will cost at tender. Every one of these answers bears directly upon the appraisal. Purchase constitutes a second decision, to be taken replacement by replacement as each falls due, in the light of the design and of the tender prices then in hand. Approval of detailed design commits the design fee together with the costs of the surveys, and nothing whatsoever beyond them. Should the design demonstrate that the duty cannot in fact be covered, or that the supply cannot be reinforced at a cost which the appraisal is able to carry, the programme halts at that point, the fleet continuing upon diesel as and when its replacements fall due.
target:
Case

The proposal is to electrify the vehicle fleet and to proceed to detailed design. The fleet works from the depot on daily rounds of deliveries and site calls, and every vehicle returns to the depot at night. That pattern is the ground of the case: vehicles that return to one base each night are charged at that base, from charging installed once and used by the whole fleet, and the daily rounds are short enough to sit within the range of the electric vehicles offered for this class of work. The depot is also where the fleet is maintained, so charging, maintenance, and parking sit on the one site. Replacement is the occasion. The vehicles in the fleet reach the end of their working lives in turn, and each replacement is a purchase that will be made in any case; electrification takes those purchases as they fall due and directs them to electric vehicles, rather than retiring serviceable vehicles early. The case does not ask the board to judge electric vehicles in general. It asks whether the fleet's own duty, run from its own depot, is the duty electric vehicles serve well, and the case is that the return-to-base pattern and the short daily rounds make it so. What the fleet gives up is the flexibility of a vehicle that can be sent anywhere at any notice on a tank filled in minutes; the detailed design stage tests the duty records against that loss before any purchase is proposed. Charging is taken overnight, while the vehicles stand in the depot and the site's own demand is at its lowest, so the charging load does not add to the peak the site draws. The drivers' working pattern does not change: vehicles leave charged in the morning and return at night, and no round in the fleet's present duty depends on refuelling away from the depot, which is the condition that makes a single charging site sufficient.

Costs

The capital cost is $1016k. The appraisal is run over a horizon of 7 years. The capital cost of $1016k covers the difference in price between the electric vehicles and the diesel vehicles they replace, the charging installation at the depot, and the electrical work the depot supply requires to carry the charging load. Within the horizon, the running costs of the electric fleet are set against those of the diesel fleet it displaces: electricity against diesel fuel, and maintenance of vehicles with fewer wearing parts against maintenance of engines, gearboxes, and exhaust treatment. The savings in the appraisal are estimates. No electric vehicle has yet run the fleet's rounds, and the consumption figures behind the savings are the makers' figures for the class, not measurements on the fleet's own duty. The appraisal records them as estimates, and the first vehicles in service give the measured figures against which the rest of the programme is judged. A shortfall in the saving acts on the appraisal of every later replacement, since each is appraised on the same basis. The vehicles are appraised over the horizon as whole vehicles: no separate value is set on the battery, and no battery replacement is charged within the horizon, the makers' cover being taken to run with the vehicle for its life in the fleet. Costs that do not change between the two fleets are excluded from both sides of the appraisal: the drivers, the depot itself, and the staff who maintain the fleet serve either fleet alike, and charging them to one side only would distort the comparison the appraisal exists to make.

Schedule

Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design: the duty records of the fleet are examined vehicle by vehicle, the depot supply is assessed, and the charging layout is fixed. Procurement follows the design, with vehicles ordered against the replacement dates the fleet already carries, so that no vehicle is bought before its predecessor falls due. The charging installation is built before the first electric vehicle arrives, and is extended as the fleet turns over. No contractor is named in the proposal; the installer is appointed by tender once the design fixes the installation. Progress is reported to the board at its regular meetings against the stages stated here. The schedule is stated in stages from approval because the replacement dates, not the project, set the pace of the changeover: the fleet is electric at the rate at which its vehicles fall due, and not faster.

Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to the purchase of vehicles. Detailed design settles the questions the case cannot: which vehicles on the market cover the fleet's longest rounds with the margin winter running requires, whether the depot supply carries the charging load of the whole fleet or must be reinforced, what the charging installation costs at tender, and what the vehicles cost at tender. Each answer acts directly on the appraisal. Purchase is a second decision, taken replacement by replacement as each falls due, on the design and the tender prices then in hand. Approval of detailed design commits the design fee and the survey costs, and nothing beyond them. If the design shows the duty cannot be covered, or the supply cannot be reinforced at a cost the appraisal carries, the programme stops there, with the fleet continuing on diesel as its replacements fall due.
